name: Harmonic-locked frequency shifter layer (shift by multiples of f0) cleaned with EQ, micro-delay and a self-vocoder
goal: Tame a frequency shifter into musical harmonics: shift by whole multiples of the note's fundamental (e.g. +130 Hz on a 130 Hz C, or 6×40 = 240 Hz on a 40 Hz E) so new partials land on the harmonic series instead of dissonant arbitrary shifts, run it as a parallel wet layer with low-cut/band-reject EQ to tame the shifted fundamental, add ~1 ms signal delay to stop bubbly phasing, and clean messy upper harmonics with a self-vocoder whose lowest band sits above the sub, keeping the clean sub on a dry path.

source.title: Chaos To Order: Frequency Shifter & Vocoder (Sound Design Tutorial)

prerequisites: Frequency shifter (coarse/fine Hz), EQ, vocoder (4–40 bands, bandwidth, formant), small signal delay, saturation
Know the fundamental frequency of the played note

inputs.name: f0_hz
inputs.description: Fundamental of the note (e.g. 130 Hz for C3, 40 Hz for E)

outputs.name: shifted_layer
outputs.description: Harmonic-aligned frequency-shift layer blended with dry

constraints: Original synthesis recipe; not affiliated with any vendor named in the source. Recreate in browser/Web Audio (Polyrhythm Studio) or any hybrid synth with comparable modules; no presets, banks or samples copied.
Shifting by non-multiples (e.g. 174 Hz on C) gives dissonant overtones — intentional only.
Harmonic alignment holds for the note whose f0 you used; other notes drift unless shift is key-tracked (implementation note).
Web Audio note (implementation, not from transcript): a frequency shifter is a Hilbert-transform single-sideband modulator (AudioWorklet).

steps.action: Start on a plain sine to learn it: note C ≈ 130 Hz. Add 130 Hz shift → up an octave; add multiples (260, 390, 520 …) and listen to each land on further harmonic-series notes (fifth, octave, third…).
Compare with an arbitrary shift (e.g. 174 Hz) to hear dissonant overtones.
Apply to a richer sound (e.g. a bass an octave down); harmonics that already line up change little, other patches gain dark, cool harmonics. Blend with the original.
Build a dry/wet split; on the wet path add EQ to tame the loud shifted 'fundamental' (low cut, or a band reject; low cut before the shifter also works).
steps.expect: Overtones without a blaring shifted fundamental

steps.action: If the layer bubbles/phases (shifts under ~1 kHz), add a ~1 ms signal delay to the path to remove it.

Clean the messy layer with a vocoder on itself: lowest band set above the sub so lows are untouched, run it on another dry/wet chain so the clean sub stays; adjust band count/bandwidth (narrower = crystalline/metallic), formant and per-band levels as EQ.
steps.expect: Tamed upper harmonics with controllable sheen

steps.action: Example bass: FM sine with modulator ×8, E at 40 Hz, shift ×6 = 240 Hz, EQ wet to keep only above ~400 Hz, vocoder, two saturators, rhythmic delay and a wash reverb; automate shifter/vocoder for performance.
Iterate non-linearly: revisit earlier FX settings after adding later ones.

verification: Shift = k×f0 sounds consonant; random Hz shift sounds dissonant on the same note.
Sub stays clean on the dry path after vocoder.
1 ms delay removes bubbly phasing on low shifts.
